[[File:Kotzig.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|Each pair of points in the left graph is connected by exactly one path of length 1, and each pair in the right graph is connected by exactly one path of length 2. These are the cases <math>k = 1</math> and <math>k = 2</math> respectively, but no graphs with <math>k\ge 3</math> have been found. {{unsolved|mathematics|Is there a finite graph on at least two vertices in which each pair of distinct vertices is connected by ''exactly one'' path of length <math>k</math>, where <math>k\ge 3</math> is fixed?}}

'''Kotzig's conjecture''' is an unproven assertion in [[graph theory]] which states that finite graphs with certain properties do not exist.
A graph is a <math>P_k</math>-graph if each pair of distinct vertices is connected by ''exactly one'' path of length <math>k</math>. Kotzig's conjecture asserts that for <math>k\ge 3</math> there are no finite <math>P_k</math>-graphs with two or more vertices. The conjecture was first formulated by [[Anton Kotzig]] in 1974.<ref name="BondyMurty1976p246"/> It has been verified for <math>k\le 20</math>,<ref name="Kostochka"/> but remains open in the general case (as of July 2026).

The conjecture is stated for <math>k\ge 3</math> because <math>P_k</math>-graphs do exist for smaller values of <math>k</math>. <math>P_1</math>-graphs are precisely the [[complete graph]]s. The [[friendship graph|friendship theorem]] states that <math>P_2</math>-graphs are precisely the (triangular) [[windmill graph]]s (that is, finitely many triangles joined at a common vertex; also known as [[friendship graph]]s).

== History ==
Kotzig's conjecture was first listed as an open problem by Bondy & Murty in 1976,<ref name="BondyMurty1976"/> attributed to Kotzig and dated to 1974.<ref name="BondyMurty1976p246"/> Kotzig's first own writing on the conjecture appeared in 1979.<ref name="KotzigSelected"/> He later verified the conjecture for <math>k\le 8</math> and claimed solution, though unpublished, for <math>k\le 9</math>.<ref name="Kotzig"/> The conjecture is now known to hold for <math>k\le 20</math> due to work of [[Alexandr Kostochka]].<ref name="Kostochka"/> Kostochka stated that his techniques extend to <math>k\le 33</math>, but a proof of this has not been published.<ref name="ProofsFromTHEBOOK"/> A survey on <math>P_k</math>-graphs was written by [[John Adrian Bondy|John A. Bondy]], including  proofs for many statements previously made by Kotzig without written proof.<ref name="Bondy"/>

In 1990 Xing & Hu claimed a proof of Kotzig's conjecture for <math>k\ge 12</math>.<ref name="XingHu"/><!-- Together with <math>9\le k\le 11</math> later verified by Yang, Lin, Wang and Li,<ref name="YangLinWangLi"/> --> This seemed to resolve the conjecture at the time, and still today leads many to believe that the problem is settled. However, Xing and Hu's proof relied on a misunderstanding of a statement proven by Kotzig. Kotzig showed that a <math>P_k</math>-graph must contain a <math>2\ell</math>-cycle for ''some'' <math>\ell\in\{3,...,k-4\}</math>,<ref name="Kotzig"/> which Xing and Hu used in the form that cycles of ''all'' these lengths must exist. 
In their paper Xing and Hu show that for <math>k\ge 12</math> a <math>P_k</math>-graph must ''not'' contain a <math>(2k-8)</math>-cycle. Since this is in contradiction to their reading of Kotzig's result, they conclude (incorrectly) that <math>P_k</math>-graphs with <math>k\ge 12</math> cannot exist. This mistake was first pointed out by Roland Häggkvist in 2000.

Kotzig's conjecture is mentioned in [[Proofs from THE BOOK]] in the chapter on the [[friendship theorem]].<ref name="ProofsFromTHEBOOK"/> It is stated that a general proof for the conjecture seems "out of reach".

== Properties of <math>P_k</math>-graphs ==
* A <math>P_k</math>-graph on <math>n</math> vertices contains precisely <math>\textstyle {n\choose 2}</math> paths of length <math>k</math>.
* Since the two end-vertices of an edge in a <math>P_k</math>-graph are connected by a unique <math>k</math>-path, each edge is contained in a unique <math>(k+1)</math>-cycle. Consequently, the graph has a unique decomposition into edge disjoint <math>(k+1)</math>-cycles, and there are no other <math>(k+1)</math>-cycles besides these. In particular, <math>P_k</math>-graphs are [[Eulerian graph|Eulerian]].<ref name="KotzigSelected"/>
* <math>P_k</math>-graphs are not [[bipartite graph|bipartite]]: if <math>k</math> is odd and <math>v,w</math> are vertices in the same bipartition class, no <math>k</math>-path can connect them. Likewise, if <math>k</math> is even and <math>v,w</math> are vertices in different bipartition classes, no <math>k</math>-path can connect them.
<!--* If <math>G</math> contains an even cycle <math>C_{2\ell}</math>, then <math>G-C_{2\ell}</math> cannot contain a path of length <math>k-\ell-1</math>.-->
* Even cycles form important substructures in <math>P_k</math>-graphs. A ''lollipop'' (not to be confused with a [[lollipop graph]]) is the union of a cycle with a path intersecting in precisely one of the end vertices of the path. If the cycle has length <math>2\ell</math>, then the path must be shorter than <math>k-\ell</math> as it would otherwise give rise to two <math>k</math>-paths with the same end vertices. Therefore, the existence and distribution of lollipops, and more generally, of even cycles, has been studied extensively. It is known that there must exist an even cycle of length <math>2\ell</math> for some <math>\ell\in\{3,...,k-5\}</math>,<ref name="Kotzig"/> and that there cannot exist even cycles of lengths <math>4</math>, <math>2k</math>, <math>2k-2</math>, <math>2k-4</math>, <math>2k-6</math><ref name="Kotzig"/> or <math>2k-8</math>.<ref name="XingHu"/>
* A <math>P_k</math>-graph cannot contain a cycle (even or odd) of length at least <math>\tfrac43 k-2</math>. At the same time, there must exist a cycle of length at least <math>k+5</math>. Combining these constraints yield <math>k\ge 21</math>.<ref name="Kostochka"/>
* Any two <math>(k+1)</math>-cycles in a <math>P_k</math>-graph must have at least three<ref name="Bondy"/> and at most <math>k-2</math><ref name="Kostochka"/> vertices in common. In particular, all <math>P_k</math>-graphs are 2-connected. Kotzig furthermore claims that any two <math>(k+1)</math>-cycles have at least ''seven'' vertices in common,<ref name="Kotzig"/> though no proof has been published.
* Let <math>c_{k+1}</math> denote the number of <math>(k+1)</math>-cycles in a given <math>P_k</math>-graph. Then <math>c_{k+1}\ge 3</math>. If <math>k</math> is even, then <math>c_{k+1}\ge 4</math>.<ref name="Kostochka"/> If <math>k</math> is odd, then <math>c_{k+1}\le \tfrac12(k-1)</math>.<ref name="Bondy"/> Consequently, the number of edges in a <math>P_k</math>-graph (for <math>k</math> odd) is bounded, and since <math>P_k</math>-graphs are connected, so is the number of vertices.
